full_judgment:
A. K. M. Sadeque, J: This Rule obtained under Section 439 and 435 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is directed legalist the judgment and order purported to have been passed on 31.9.85 by Mr. M.A. Mannan Miah, Magistrate 1st Class, Sadar Rajshahi discharging 'opposite party No.1 and 2 under section 119 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in Criminal Misc. Case No. 15- M of 1984 under section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure: 

 2. The Criminal Misc. Case No. 15-M of 1984 under section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was initiated by a petition of complaint dated 22.2.84 filed by complainant petitioner in the Court of City Magistrate, Rajshahi on the allegation inter-alia, that the petitioner is an inhabitant of Begum Rokeya Road, Hatem Khan, Ward No.7, Municipal Holding No. 393 in the town of Rajshahi. The opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 namely, Golam Mostafa @ Dulal and Mst. Zaheda Banu Bibi live adjacent south of his residence, there being a partition wall between the two houses. The opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and at their instigation their Bharatias have been putting dirty clothes etc. upon the boundary wall. They also throw refuses and various kinds of nasty things in the compound of the petitioner, causing an obnoxious atmosphere in the petitioner's premises. The petitioner and his family members asked the opposite parties to refrain from causing the nuisance in their premises. At this the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 became angry and abused them in filthy language and held out serious threats. On 22.2.84 at about 8-30 A.M. the opposite parties No.1 and 2 and their Bharatias, accompanied by several goondas knocked upon the door of the residence of the petitioner and announced threats to murder them. The petitioner and their family members, therefore, had genuine apprehension that the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 with the help of the charities and hired goondas would materialize their threats. The petitioner works as the Deputy Attorney-General in the High Court Division of Rangpur Bench and the family members of the petitioner are in constant trepidation. The opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 therefore should be bound down under the provision of section 107 of the Code or Criminal Procedure for keeping peace and safety or the petitioner and his family members. 

 3. The trial Magistrate served the opposite parties with notice to show cause why they should not be bound down to bond of Tk. 2,000/- for keeping peace and maintaining safety and security of the petitioner and the members of his family. The opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 appeared before the learned Magistrate. Upon being examined under section 242 Cr. P.C. the opposite parties No. 1 and 2 pleaded innocence. In the proceeding the petitioner examined 3 witnesses including himself, and the opposite parties examined one witness. The learned Magistrate on consideration of the evidence on record came to a finding that the petitioner had previous enmity with the opposite parties Nos. 1 and 2 and had concocted the case taking the advantage of his high official position. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order passed by the learned Magistrate discharging the opposite parties under section 119 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the complainant has obtained this Rule. 

 4. Mr. Amin Azhar, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted at the outset the manner in which the learned Magistrate held the proceeding and arrived at his conclusion would indicate that the judicial mind was tainted with bias and the petitioner's cause did not receive a fair consideration from him. He has drawn my attention to annexure 6 an information slip which shows that the judgment in question was delivered on 3.8.85, though the judgment is dated 31.8.85 and the corresponding 'Order sheet saying that judgment is delivered is dated 31.8.85./1.9.85. The learned Advocate therefore, argued that the dates in the judgment and order sheet have been subsequently interpolated and the judgment was not pronounced, signed and dated in the open court as required u/S 366, 367(1) and 369 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and so the impugned judgment is no judgment in the eye of law. He also submits that there has been an unseemly delay in the delivery of the judgment, for the arguments in the case, as the order sheet will show, were heard as far back as on 17.7.85; and this also reflects upon the manner in which the learned Magistrate dealt with the proceeding before him. The learned Advocate points out that the complainant had made an application on 27.6.85 to the effect that he as the deputy Attorney-General, Rangpur was busy with his official matters and would not be able to turn 'up' before the Court on the next date, because on account of the conduct of the opposite parties adjournment had been necessitated, although the petitioner’s witnesses were examined and cross examined. He sought to be represented by his Advocate Abul Kalam Azad in the subsequent dates. The learned Magistrate far from granting this privilege to the complainant, which was due to him as a public servant under the proviso to the Sec. 247 of the Cr.P.C. had only passed the order "not admitted." The learned Magistrate did not even care to reject the petition with reasons. On the other hand it is pointed out the learned Magistrate granted time to the opposite parties on 16.6.85, though the opposite parties made no application or Tadbir for their absence, stating reasons for their absence. 

 5. Again it has been brought to my notice that the complainant had made petition time and again that the opposite parties had held out threat to and suborned the witnesses or the complainant, so that he was not able to bring them to depose on his behalf viz. petition dated 9.10.84 and 19.2.85 etc. But the learned Magistrate did not take any measures for protection or the witnesses and enabling them to depose before the Court on behalf of the complainant petitioner. Again the learned Advocate submitted the learned Magistrate on account of his bias did not refrain from making caustic and uncharitable remarks in the judgment itself about the complainant. The learned Magistrate has remarked at page 6 of his judgment as follows:- বাদী একজন উচ্চ পদস্থ কর্মচারী এবং যিনি প্রয়োজন এই মামলার সৃষ্টি করিয়াছেন বলিয়া প্রতিয়মান প্রতিবাদীর জেরায় বলা হ���য়াছে যাহা যথার্থ বলিয়াই মনে হয়।" It is submitted and it also appears from the deposition or the D.W. 1 Zinnath that even the D.W. 1 did not accuse the complainant to have taken the advantage of his high position to concoct this case. From these it has been urged by the learned Advocate  for the complainant petitioner it appears that the learned Magistrate had a definite bias against the complainant petitioner. A perusal of an entire record and particularly the above aspects of the proceeding tend to convince one that the learned Magistrate had a bias against the complainant petitioner. But before coming to such a finding it is necessary to examine if the conclusions arrived at by the learned Magistrate are wrong and insupportable by evidence and law 

 6. Now so far as the appraisal of the evidence is concerned I am of the,view that the learned Magistrate has not properly assessed the same. J have been taken through the deposition of the witnesses for the complainant petitioner and also of the opposite party. The P.W.1, Sultan Ahmed is the complainant himself. He is the Deputy Attorney-General of the Supreme Court and holds a high respectable position. He has given the case and borne out the incident which has raised the apprehension about the future conduct of the opposite parties. His evidence was discredited by the learned Magistrate on the ground that he did not make any G.D. Entry about the incident alleged by him. It is not understandable why G.D. Entry should be necessary when the petitioner has brought the instant case. A suggestion was given to the complainant that he had brought the present proceeding on account of previous enmity and pendency of Civil litigation between him and the opposite parties. This suggestion rather gives a motive for the conduct of opposite parties. The opposite parties are apt to hold out threats and to behave as they did with the complainant petitioner on account of the previous enmity. P.W. 2 M.A. Kader is also a respectable witness being a retired Govt. Official. He has stated that in the month of February, 1984 he had heard a row near the house of the O.Ps. and the complainant. He appears to be a close neighbour of the parties. As against this, the opposite parties examined one Zinnat Ali as D.W. 1. This witness as it appears from his cross-examination comes from Sirajgonj and was the bharatia of the opposite parties. This witness is obviously an interested witness. Little reliance can be placed on the evidence of this witness. Therefore it is seen that the preponderance of the evidence is in support of the allegation of threats offered to the petitioner and his family members. The complainant petitioner generally lives away from home in connection with his calling, and his family should be considered left in the lurch and at the mercy of the opposite parties. 

 7. It appears that the complainant had in- formed the learned Magistrate by a petition dated 23.2.85 that the opposite parties had broken the boundary wall and held out threats to the family of the complainant and he had been obliged to bring a case under section 447 of the Penal Code against the opposite parties on 19.2.85. At this hearing the learned Advocate for the complainant petitioner has filed the certified copy of the judgment of the Criminal Revision No. 26 of 1986 to show that the complainant petitioner brought against the opposite parties a Criminal case which was numbered as G.R. Case No. 89/85 under sections 447, 427 and 341 Cr. P.C. The accused were released in accordance with section 339C of the Code of the Criminal Procedure for lapse of time. The order of release was set aside by a Division Bench of this Court with direction to proceed afresh with the G.R. Case No. 89 of 1985. This fact shows that the apprehension of the complainant petitioner was not unfounded. 

 8. From the aforesaid facts and circumstances and the evident on record I find that the learned Magistrate did not base his findings on proper appreciation of evidence on record and was rather biased against the complainant petitioner for reasons unknown although there is nothing to show that the learned Magistrate had personal interest in the case the manner in which he has conducted the proceeding of the case manifests his bias. The impugned order of the learned Magistrate which is unsupported by the evidence and tainted with bias cannot be sustained. 

 9. I am aware that under provisional jurisdiction the occasion to interfere with an order of discharge under section 119 of the Criminal Procedure Code should be rare, particularly at the instance of a private party. But in the instant case bias has been so patent on the part of the learned Magistrate that this Court finds it appropriate to interfere with his impugned order. The impugned order should be set aside. Again, in view of the bias of the learned Magistrate I find it expedient to pass an order binding down the opposite parties to keep peace without sending the case back on remand to him. It was submitted with cogent reason that the remarks passed against complainant petitioner in the judgment and order as quoted above should be expunged.
